PCSK9 inhibition and atherosclerotic 
cardiovascular disease prevention: does reality 
match the hype?
Savvas Hadjiphilippou,1 Kausik K Ray2
Abstract
Within this review we look at whether the potential 
provided by proprotein convertase subtilisin/
kexin type 9 (PCSK9) inhibition for prevention of 
atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease matches the 
excitement generated. Two fully human monoclonal 
antibodies to PCSK9 are currently licenced for clinical 
use both in the USA and the European Union: 
evolocumab and alirocumab. These reduce low-density 
lipoprotein cholesterol by over 50% across a range of 
populations and were generally found to have a safety 
profile comparable with placebo. The development 
programme for a third humanised monoclonal 
antibody, bococizumab, was terminated early due to 
the presence of neutralising antibodies reducing its 
efficacy over time. Results from the first cardiovascular 
outcomes trial, FOURIER, have demonstrated significant 
reductions in cardiovascular events in a population 
with stable cardiovascular disease over a 2-year period. 
The ODYSSEY OUTCOMES trial comparing alirocumab 
to placebo is expected to report in 2018 and provide 
cardiovascular outcome data in a post acute coronary 
syndrome population. Monoclonal antibodies have 
an injection burden of 12–26 injections per year. An 
alternative approach to reducing PCSK9 is to inhibit 
translation of the messenger RNA for PCSK9. The phase 
II ORION-1 study using inclisiran, a small interference 
RNA to PCSK9, suggested that two doses of inclisiran 
produced time averaged reductions in LDL cholesterol 
of 50% over 9 months. The ORION-4 cardiovascular 
outcome trial will assess the cardiovascular benefits 
of two injections per year using inclisiran. With further 
outcome trials expected, appropriate patient selection 
will be key considering the higher drug costs of these 
therapies.
Introduction
Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) is a 
causal factor in developing atherosclerotic heart 
disease.1 2 Within the cholesterol metabolism pathway 
(figure 1), proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 
9 (PCSK9) is a serine protease encoded by a single gene 
that undergoes processing within the endoplasmic 
reticulum predominantly of hepatocytes. Attach-
ment of PCSK9 to the LDL receptor (LDL-R) leads 
to internalisation of both in clathrin-coated endo-
somes and triggers the enzymatic degradation of the 
LDL-R resulting in reduced LDL-R numbers on the 
cell surface.3 4 Since its discovery in 2003, the PCSK9 
pathway has rapidly come to centre stage from a basic 
understanding of its biology and its putative causal 
role in cardiovascular disease (CVD) to become the 
next therapeutic target in CVD prevention.1
PCSK9 discovery and evolution
Discovery of PCSK9
Familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH) is an auto-
somal dominant genetic disorder. Until 2003, 
genetic defects present in genes encoding the LDL-R 
or apolipoprotein B were known to cause autosomal 
dominant hypercholesterolaemia. Genetic studies5 6 
identified cases of FH not clearly linked to either 
mutations in the LDL-R or ApoB gene, suggesting 
a third genetic locus responsible for FH. Following 
work by Abifadel et al7 a further two mutations 
in the gene encoding PCSK9 were discovered and 
found to also cause autosomal dominant hypercho-
lesterolaemia (figure 2).
PCKS9 inhibition
A number of different approaches are currently 
being trialled for PCSK9 inhibition (tables  1 and 
28–11); monoclonal antibodies (mAbs), small protein 
inhibitors (peptides/adnectins) and gene silencing 
using antisense oligonucleotides (ASO) or small 
interfering RNA (siRNA). Of these, the only drug 
therapy licenced for use both in the USA and Euro-
pean Union is mAb therapy. Monoclonal antibodies 
and small protein inhibitors (peptides/adnectins) 
work extracellularly by targeting circulating PCSK9 
either by sequestering circulating PCSK9 (mAbs) 
or blocking the binding of PCSK9 to the LDL-R 
(peptides/adnectins). Gene silencing techniques 
using ASO or siRNA target intracellular PCSK9 
production at the level of translation.
Monoclonal antibodies
Monoclonal antibodies are antibodies that bind to a 
specific epitope on an antigen. The first therapeutic 
mAbs were made from mouse protein; however, 
their short elimination half-life limited their use in 
the long term. Subsequent compositions consisted 
of chimeric antibodies (65% human), humanised 
(>90% human) and human (100% human).
Three mAbs have been in development 
targeting PCSK9; however, only two are currently 
licenced. Two are fully human mAb: alirocumab, 
which is developed by Sanofi and Regeneron, and 
evolocumab, which is developed by Amgen. The 
third is a humanised mAb called bococizumab 
produced by Pfizer. While a phase III trial for 
bococizumab was recruiting, in November of 
2016, Pfizer withdrew this drug from develop-
ment due to the presence of antidrug neutralising 
antibodies that reduced drug efficacy over time.

molecules that act via the RNA-induced silencing complex.

phase 1 human trial of an RNA interference of PCSK9 demon-
strated a 70% reduction in PCSK9 levels and 40% reduction in 
LDL-C over 84 days.14 Results were statistically significant, and 
overall the drug was well tolerated.
In 2017 the results of ORION-1 were published.15 In this 
phase II double-blind, placebo-controlled, multiple ascend-
ing-dose clinical trial of 501 patients, those patients who received 
inclisiran had dose-dependent reductions in PCSK9 and LDL-C. 
The greatest reduction in LDL-C was observed in the two-dose 
300 mg regimen (at days 1 and 90) with a mean LDL-C reduction 
of 52.6% and up to 81% at 6 months. All patients in this group 
responded with significant LDL-C lowering. Importantly, there 
were no clinically significant effects on liver function relating to 
the drug, and it was well tolerated. The sustained response to 
LDL-C reduction in the two-dose regimen highlights the issue 
of injection frequency and raises the possibility of a reduced 
injection burden as compared with mAb therapy. ORION-4 will 
be the cardiovascular outcomes trial of inclisiran in high-risk 
primary and secondary prevention patients with average LDL-C 
of approximately 3.36 mmol/L.
Populations studied
CVD and high LDL-C
The largest patient population studied are those with estab-
lished CVD or at high risk of CVD that has failed to reach target 
LDL-C levels despite statin and other lipid-lowering therapy. In 
this group of patients both alirocumab and evolocumab have 
demonstrated significant reductions in LDL-C (figures  315–22 
and 4).23–27 Dosing of evolocumab and alirocumab follows 
different strategies.28–32 For evolocumab the aim is to achieve 
the greatest reduction in LDL-C and so this is either adminis-
tered as a biweekly dose of 140 mg (1 mL) or monthly dose of 
420 mg (3 mL) both achieving the same levels in LDL reduction. 
Development of the dosing regimen of alirocumab has followed 
a treat to target approach with dosing beginning at 75 mg every 
2 weeks, increased to 150 mg every 2 weeks if LDL-C reduction 
does not reach target levels. Aside from reductions in LDL-C, 
significant changes in other lipid parameters were also noted 
(figure 5); however, it is unclear what the clinical significance is 
of these changes.
Familial hypercholesterolaemia
Patients with FH are a subgroup of patients with increased risk of 
atherosclerotic CVD even on maximally tolerated statin therapy.33 
Few patients with FH reach LDL-C targets, and the addition of 
non-statin therapy is often required. Regardless of the type of 
genetic mutation resulting in autosomal dominant FH, carriers 
have a significantly increased risk for coronary artery disease.34 
Determining which patients to initiate non-statin therapy to is 
predominantly based on failure to reach target LDL-C levels. Both 
alirocumab and evolocumab have been shown to be effective in 
reducing LDL-C in patients with heterozygous FH and attaining 
LDL-C targets previously unachievable with statins alone or 
statins plus ezetimibe irrespective of the type of genetic mutation. 
For patients with homozygous FH, treatment is even more chal-
lenging, and lipoprotein apheresis is often used as further therapy. 
Lipoprotein apheresis removes apoB100 from the blood; however, 
this treatment has to be performed regularly as LDL-C levels 
rapidly recover to baseline between sessions.35 36 Evolocumab is 
the only PCSK9 inhibitor so far studied specifically within this 
group of patients (TESLA part B trial), and the TAUSSIG trial 
is ongoing and is assessing the long-term safety and efficacy of 
evolocumab in patients with homozygous FH at 5 years.
Statin intolerance
Statin intolerance among patients remains a real concern as it 
limits therapy. This is particularly relevant in those patient groups

PROFICIO (Program to Reduce LDL-C and Cardiovascular Outcomes Following Inhibition of PCSK9 in Different Populations) is the clinical trial programme evaluating evolocumab, which includes 20 clinical trials. Of these, 14 trials are phase 
III trials evaluating evolocumab in high-risk patients including those who are intolerant to statins, having a diagnosis of heterozygous and homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia or poor LDL-C response even with high-intensity statin or 
non-statin treatment. Five studies in the phase III programme provide long-term safety and efficacy data: FOURIER (Further Cardiovascular OUtcomes Research with PCSK9 Inhibition in Subjects with Elevated Risk), DESCARTES (Durable Effect of

alirocumab in combination with other lipid-lowering drugs or as monotherapy across a wide range of patients including those with high cardiovascular risk, those unable to tolerate statin therapy and patients with heterozygous FH who are 
inadequately controlled by current lipid therapy. While phase II patients were those with primary hypercholesterolaemia on stable statin doses, the Phase III cohort includes patients intolerant of statins and those on no therapy at all.

events such as in FH as traditional non-statin alternatives are not 
as efficacious. Rates of reported muscle symptoms in patients on 
statins are variable; however, this does not reflect causality with 
statin therapy, and thus the relationship to statins is uncertain. 
In routine clinical practice, however, patients may discontinue 
statin therapy regardless of whether there is a causal relationship 
or not. Four trials have specifically studied PCSK9 inhibitors 
in patients intolerant of statins (Figures 3,4). Within the statin 
intolerant subgroup, both alirocumab and evolocumab demon-
strated significantly greater reductions in LDL-C compared with 
ezetimibe alone.
Safety
General
From a safety perspective, reported adverse events leading to 
discontinuation of treatment are low and similar between treat-
ment arms and control groups.37 38 Commonly reported adverse 
events include nasopharyngitis, upper respiratory tract infec-
tions and headache. Injection site reactions were generally mild 
and self-limiting.19 25
The OSLER studies38 were open-label studies evaluating the 
efficacy and safety of long-term administration of evolocumab 
(approximately 2 years). Reassuringly the incidence of adverse 
events was not significantly increased with evolocumab or 
among those who reached low LDL-C levels. In the ODYSSEY 
LONG TERM study, similarly low rates of adverse events have 
been demonstrated when using alirocumab.23
Neurocognitive
Monoclonal  antibody inhibitors to PCSK9 are too large to 
cross the blood–brain barrier. Despite this, concerns regarding 
the impact of PCSK9 inhibitors on cognitive function were 
raised. A recent meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials in 
assessing PCSK9 inhibitors against other lipid-lowering therapies 
concluded that while PCSK9 inhibition significantly improved 
lipid profiles and reduced the incidence of all-cause mortality 
compared with placebo, this was associated with a higher rate of 
neurocognitive adverse events.39 The EBBINGHAUS cognitive 
function study (Evaluating PCSK9 Binding antiBody Influence 
oN coGnitive HeAlth in High cardiovascUlar Risk Subjects) 
investigated potential neurocognitive effects from evolocumab 
treatment. This double-blind placebo-controlled randomised 
non-inferiority trial involved 1974 patients enrolled in the 
FOURIER outcomes study. Patients were already on moderate or 
high-intensity statins and received evolocumab 140 mg every 2 
weeks or 420 mg every month or placebo. The primary endpoint 
was executive function measured using the Cambridge Neuro-
psychological Test Automated Battery and secondary endpoints 
were working memory, memory function and psychomotor 
speed. Follow-up was for 20 months.40 Results presented at 
the recent American College of Cardiology Congress demon-
strated no significant difference in the primary and secondary 
endpoints between the evolocumab and placebo groups. In addi-
tion, patients who had very low LDL levels (0.65 mmol/L) did 
not have worsening of cognitive function.41 Considering that 
patients are usually treated with lipid-lowering medication for 
long periods of time, this trial had a short follow-up period. 
An open-label extension trial is therefore planned to evaluate 
safety further in 6000 FOURIER participants within which all 
EBBINGHAUS participants will be included.
Antidrug-neutralising antibodies
In non-fully human mAbs immunogenicity can lead to the devel-
opment of antidrug antibodies (ADA). Neutralising antibodies 
are a type of antidrug antibody (ADA) that reduce the efficacy 
of drug therapy.
With a 3% murine sequence in the humanised mAb bococi-
zumab, the risk of immunogenicity was increased compared with 
fully human mAbs and this resulted in the formation of neutral-
ising ADA, which attenuated the effect of LDL-C reduction. In 
the six multinational lipid-lowering Studies of PCSK9 Inhibition 
and the Reduction of Vascular Events (SPIRE) programme for 
the development of bococizumab, the magnitude of per  cent 
reduction in LDL reduction at 52 weeks was attenuated in all 
1-year SPIRE trials. At 1 year, 48% of patients who received 
bococizumab had detectable ADAs and 29% developed neutral-
ising antibodies.12
By contrast, very low rates of immunogenicity were observed 
in clinical trials of alirocumab. Using data from 10 ODYSSEY 
trials, ADAs were observed in 5.1% of patients administered 
alirocumab, but only 1.4% had persistent ADA (>2 consecutive 
positive samples over >12 weeks) and 1.3% of patients were 
observed to have neutralising antibodies.42 Reductions in LDL-C 
levels however were maintained regardless of ADA status. In the 
FOURIER trial, ADAs to evolocumab were rarely detected, and 
there were no neutralising antibodies seen.43
Effects on atherosclerosis regression
The GLAGOV trial investigated the effects of evolocumab on 
progression of coronary disease.44 This multicentre trial recruited 
968 patients to either evolocumab 420 mg monthly for 78 weeks

Antisense oligonucleotides (ASO)
ASOs are single stranded synthetic polymers of modified deoxynucleotides or ribonucleotides. These interfere with 
gene transcription through direct binding of mRNA8 blocking the target mRNA from being translated. A phase I 
human clinical trial with nucleic acid antisense inhibitor of PCSK9 demonstrated a significant reduction in LDL-C 
compared with placebo; however, this was also associated with a significant increase in acute kidney injury and signs 
of renal tubular toxicity.9 The clinical development of this ASO was therefore terminated although others are still in 
development.
Small protein inhibitors
Small protein inhibitors such as peptides and adnectins work by directly inhibiting PCSK9 interaction with the 
LDL-R. PCSK9 binds to the LDL-R through an epidermal growth factor-like repeat A (EGF-A) domain. An animal study 
using a peptide mimicking the EGF-A domain on the LDL-R, thus inhibiting PCSK9 from binding, demonstrated a 
30%–50% reduction in LDL-C levels.10 Adnectins are synthetic proteins used as alternatives to antibodies for target 
therapy. This technology has been under development by Bristol-Myers-Squibb. In a human study of BMS-962476, an 
adnectin-based protein inhibitor of PCSK9 binding to the LDL-R a reduction of up to 48% in LDL-C was documented.11 
Small protein inhibitors have the potential of being developed for oral administration and therefore avoid the need 
for frequent injections. Further work however is required in order to avoid enzymatic degradation by gut enzymes and 
to ensure therapy is equally specific in its target as monoclonal antibodies.

more than 50% in evolocumab-treated patients. Primary efficacy 
measure was the change in per cent atheroma volume (PAV) from 
baseline to week 78, measured using intravascular ultrasonog-
raphy imaging. Results demonstrated a 0.95% reduction in PAV 
from baseline in the evolocumab group compared with a 0.05% 
increase in PAV in the placebo group. Interestingly, 1/3 of patients 
did not show plaque regression despite evolocumab therapy 
suggesting that plaque regression may be multifactorial. The 
results of the GLAGOV trial were less than predicted when taking 
into consideration what is already known based on the regression 
line for LDL-C reduction and percentage reduction in atheroma 
volume. This may relate to the presence of other risk factors in 
the baseline characteristics of the population studied (smoking, 
diabetes and increased body mass index) that may mitigate some 
of the effects of LDL-C reduction, as these factors would not be 
directly affected by LDL-C reduction. This reinforces the need 
for a multifactorial approach and controlling all risk factors to 
optimise atherosclerosis regression. In addition, previous model-
ling studies have suggested that a greater change in clinical risk 
observed per unit change in atheroma burden was seen in those 
with the least disease at baseline.45 Subgroup analysis of the 
GLAGOV population showed that the largest regression was seen 
in those who already had low LDL-C <1.8 mmol/L after statin 
therapy and therefore achieved the lowest on-treatment LDL-C 
after the addition of evolocumab (<1.0 mmol/L).
Cardiovascular outcomes
One of the main questions in the field of PCSK9 inhibition has 
been whether reductions in LDL-C levels by PCSK9 inhibitors

placebo, evolocumab led to a statistically significant reduction in LDL-C in both groups at 12 weeks (59.2% in the biweekly dosing regimen and 
61.3% in the monthly dosing regimen).19 Significant reductions were observed among patients irrespective of mutation type (LDL-R, ApoB, PCSK9). 
In the TESLA part B trial (Trial Evaluating PCSK9 Antibody in Subjects With LDL Receptor Abnormalities), evolocumab demonstrated reductions in

Findings from a small post hoc analysis of the ODYSSEY LONG

ODYSSEY OUTCOMES trial is the cardiovascular outcomes

bo-controlled trial in patients who have experienced an acute 
coronary syndrome  (ACS) event 4–52 weeks prior to rando-

coronary heart disease death, acute myocardial infarction, 
hospitalisation for unstable angina or ischaemic stroke. In this 
trial, patients received injections of alirocumab (75–150 mg) or 
matching placebo while also on maximally tolerated standard 
lipid-lowering therapy. In comparison with FOURIER, this trial 
specifically studies a recent ACS population rather than those 
with stable coronary artery disease. In ODYSSEY OUTCOMES, 
89.5% of patients were on high intensity statins compared with 
69.2% in FOURIER. In addition, endpoints studied are specific 
to coronary artery disease and ischaemic stroke rather than CVD 
and stroke (including haemorrhagic stroke), as was the case with 
FOURIER, with a longer median follow-up of 33 months.
Results from the SPIRE cardiovascular outcome trials studying 
bococizumab were recently reported.48 Unfortunately, due to the 
discontinuation of the bococizumab development programme, 
both these trials were stopped early. In these two parallel trials 
with different entry criteria for LDL-C, 27 438 patients were 
assigned to receive either bococizumab 150 mg subcutaneously 
every 2 weeks or placebo. Primary endpoint was non-fatal 
myocardial infarction, non-fatal stroke, hospitalisation for 
unstable angina requiring urgent revascularisation or cardio-
vascular death. Of note 93% of patients were receiving statin 
therapy at baseline. In SPIRE-1, patients had a baseline LDL-C 
of ≥1.8 mmol/L and median follow-up was for 7 months. No 
significant difference was noted in MACE. In SPIRE-2, patients 
had a baseline LDL-C of ≥2.6 mmol/L and median follow-up 
was 12 months. In this higher risk patient cohort with longer 
follow-up, bococizumab was associated with a significant reduc-
tion in primary and secondary endpoints. While bococuzimab 
development has been discontinued, SPIRE-2 provides support 
for the FOURIER findings.

of patients at high risk of progressive atherosclerotic CVD are 
patients with FH. Treatment of FH is challenging. Despite stan-
dard therapy patients often fail to reach target LDL-C levels and, 
in addition, their pharmacological treatment may be limited by 
intolerance to higher doses of existing therapies, principally 
statins. Another group of patients are those with established 
coronary artery disease with elevated LDL-C levels despite being 
on maximally tolerated medical therapy (statin/ezetimibe).
In a recent paper by Robinson et al,33 a quantitative approach 
to determine those who might benefit most from treatment with 
non-statin drugs has been postulated. This approach determined 
patient’s absolute risk and incorporated the estimated per cent 
LDL-C reduction for ezetimibe (20%), PCSK9 inhibition (50% 
or 65%) to calculate numbers needed to treat (NNT). In high-
risk patients (>30% 10-year risk despite statin therapy), the 
addition of ezetimibe would require NNT of <50, for patients 
with LDL-C levels of  >3.4 mmol/L. This is compared with 
NNT<30 for PCSK9 inhibition (65% lowering) even when LDL 
levels on statin are 1.8 mmol/L. The paper suggests that addi-
tion of PCSK9 inhibitors to maximally tolerated statin therapy 
may be cost-effective in high-risk and very high-risk patients 
depending on their baseline LDL-C levels, absolute levels of risk 
and pricing.
Conclusion
Since rapidly coming to the forefront of lipid therapy, PCSK9 
inhibition has demonstrated efficacy in reducing LDL-C levels 
on top of standard medical therapy as well as monotherapy in 
those intolerant of statins. This is particularly relevant in high-
risk patients such as those with established coronary artery 
disease or with underlying genetic mutations predisposing to 
high levels of LDL-C and consequently increased risk of prema-
ture atherosclerotic CVD. Results from FOURIER confirm 
significant reductions in major adverse cardiovascular events 
with PCSK9 inhibition. Therapy is well tolerated with no wors-
ening of cognitive function as a result of reduced LDL-C. Results 
from ODYSSEY OUTCOMES are eagerly anticipated and will 
help further in guiding treatment through appropriate patient 
selection given the cost of therapy.
